name: Design a GraphQL Federation Gateway
intent: Let clients ask one GraphQL question across many teams' services, and answer it with a few batched calls, within a cost budget, without any team being able to break the others.
codeTitle: a query planner with batched entity fetches, cost limits and persisted queries
finalIntro: One app screen asking for users, their orders and each order's product.
prompt: Design a GraphQL gateway for a company where the users, orders and products teams each run their own service. Mobile and web apps send one query that spans all three. Teams must deploy their schemas independently, the gateway must not turn one query into hundreds of backend calls, and one expensive query must not take everything down.
functional: Present one schema to clients, built from the schemas of many teams' services
Split each query into the parts each service owns, and join the answers
Let one service extend a type owned by another, such as orders adding to User
Reject queries that are too deep or too expensive
Accept queries by stored id, so apps send a hash and not the text
Block a schema change that would break a client in use
nonFunctional: A typical screen query takes about 100 ms at the 99th percentile on top of the slowest service
The number of backend calls for a query depends on its depth, not on how many items it returns
Thousands of queries per second at the peak
One slow or failing service degrades only the fields it owns
Teams deploy independently, and a bad schema change is caught before it goes live
Abusive queries are cheap to reject, before any service does work

firstAttempt.text: One GraphQL server holds the whole schema. Every field has a resolver, and a resolver calls the owning team's service for the parent object in front of it. A query for users, their orders and each order's product walks the tree, field by field.
limits: A list of 10 users with 10 orders each makes 1 + 10 + 100 calls, because each parent object triggers its own call (the N+1 problem)
Every team must change the one codebase and deploy it together, so the teams are no longer independent
Nothing stops a query that asks for friends of friends of friends, which can touch millions of objects
Large query texts are sent on every request, and anyone can send any query
One slow service slows every resolver that waits on it

steps.title: Compose the teams' schemas into one supergraph
steps.problem: One shared codebase means every team waits for the others, but clients want a single schema and a single endpoint.
steps.fix: Each team runs its own service (a subgraph) with its own schema, and marks the types it owns with a key, such as User by id. A composition step reads all the subgraph schemas, checks that they fit together, and produces one supergraph schema that says which service owns each field. A router loads that supergraph and presents it to clients as a single GraphQL endpoint. One service can extend a type owned by another: the orders service adds an 'orders' field to User by naming the key and nothing more.
steps.tradeoff: Teams own their part and deploy alone, and clients see one schema. Composition becomes a build step that can fail, the shared types need agreed keys, and there is a new component, the router, that every request passes through.

steps.title: Plan each query across the services
steps.problem: A query such as users, their orders and each order's product touches three services, and the router has to decide in what order to ask them.
steps.fix: The query planner reads the supergraph and the query, and builds a plan: a tree of fetches. The first fetch asks the users service for the users and their keys. A second fetch sends those keys to the orders service. A third sends the product keys from the orders to the products service. Fetches that do not depend on each other run in parallel, and each fetch asks for only the fields the client wants. The router then merges the pieces into the shape the client asked for. Plans are cached by query, so repeated queries skip the planning.
steps.tradeoff: The client writes one query, and the plan does the least work that gives the answer. The plan has as many sequential rounds as the query has levels, and each round pays a network round trip, so very deep queries are slow even when each call is fast.

steps.title: Fetch entities in batches, not one by one
steps.problem: With 10 users and 10 orders each, a fetch per parent object makes 1 + 10 + 100 calls, and the number grows with the size of the answer.
steps.fix: A service that extends a type exposes one entity lookup (a query that returns objects by their keys) that takes a list of keys, and the router sends all the keys of one level in one call. A batching window collects the keys that arrive within a millisecond or so, removes duplicates and sends one request per service and level. The response comes back as a list in the same order as the keys, and is spread back to the parents. The same idea inside a service, a data loader, avoids N+1 against its own database. The number of calls now depends on the depth of the query: for the example it is 3, whether there are 10 users or 1,000.
steps.tradeoff: Calls fall from hundreds to a handful, and work for repeated keys is done once. A batch has to wait for the slowest key, a very large batch needs a size cap, and one failing key must not fail the whole batch, so the answer is per key.

steps.title: Limit query depth and cost before running anything
steps.problem: GraphQL lets a client ask for friends of friends of friends, and one such query can touch millions of objects.
steps.fix: Before planning, a guard analyses the query. It rejects a query deeper than a set depth, and it estimates the cost: each list field multiplies the number of objects by its expected size (or by its 'first' argument, the page size, which must be capped), and the cost is the sum over all the fields. A query above the budget gets an error without any service being called. Cost can also be charged to the caller's rate limit, so heavy queries use up an allowance faster than light ones. Real cost can be recorded afterwards to correct the estimates.
steps.tradeoff: Abusive queries are rejected in microseconds, and the budget gives clients a clear rule. Depth alone is not enough, since a shallow query with wide lists can still be huge, and the estimates are guesses that sometimes reject a legitimate query or let through a costly one.

steps.title: Accept persisted queries by hash
steps.problem: Apps send the full text of large queries on every request, and any caller can send any query at all.
steps.fix: The build of each app extracts its queries and uploads them to a store, keyed by a hash of the text. At runtime the app sends only the hash and the variables, which is smaller and can use a plain GET that a CDN may cache. In the strict mode the gateway runs only queries whose hash is in the store, so a public caller cannot invent an expensive query. Queries and their analysed cost and plan are looked up once and kept. A softer mode, automatic persisted queries, lets the first request register the text, and is useful for trusted apps.
steps.tradeoff: Requests are smaller and cacheable, and the set of queries that can ever run is known and can be tested in advance. Every app release must publish its queries first, and ad hoc exploration needs a separate path for trusted developers.

steps.title: Check every schema change before it ships
steps.problem: A team renames a field or makes it required, and a version of an app in the field that still uses the old shape breaks.
steps.fix: A change to a subgraph schema is first sent to the registry for a check. The check composes the new subgraph with the others, to make sure the supergraph is still valid, and then compares the result with the operations that clients actually ran in the last weeks, taken from the usage records. Removing a field that is still used is blocked. Additive changes pass. A passing change is published and rolled out, often to a few routers first, and the router can serve the old supergraph until the new one is ready. Fields are deprecated first and removed once their usage reaches zero.
steps.tradeoff: Teams can change their schema often and safely, and breaking changes are caught in review and not in production. Safety depends on good usage data, and old app versions that never go away hold fields in place for a long time.

failures.scenario: The products service is slow or down
failures.impact: Every query that includes a product waits for it, and the router's connections fill up with waiting requests.
failures.answer: Each fetch has a deadline, and a circuit breaker stops calls to a service that keeps failing. Fields from a failed service become null with an error entry, so the rest of the answer still arrives if the field is nullable in the schema. Each service has its own limited pool of connections, so one slow service cannot use up the pool of the others.

failures.scenario: A query is within the depth limit but asks for huge lists
failures.impact: Three levels deep with 1,000 items per list touches a billion objects, and a depth limit alone does not notice.
failures.answer: The cost estimate multiplies the list sizes, so the query is rejected before any call. A list field must have a capped page size argument, and clients page through large results instead of asking for them all at once.

failures.scenario: A team deploys a schema that does not compose
failures.impact: If the new schema were loaded as it is, the supergraph would be invalid and the router could fail for every client.
failures.answer: Composition runs in the schema check before the change is published. A router keeps serving the last good supergraph, and loads a new one only after it has been composed and validated. A bad deployment stays inside the team that made it.

failures.scenario: One query is much slower than expected and nobody knows where the time went
failures.impact: The router and three services each contribute, and without a view of the whole query the slow part is a guess.
failures.answer: The router starts a trace for each request and passes its id to every fetch, so the trace shows the plan with the time of each call. Metrics per field and per service show which part of the supergraph is slow, and the slowest queries are listed by their hash.

alternatives.title: How to combine teams' schemas

options.name: One schema in one server
options.con: All teams share one codebase and one deployment

options.name: Schema stitching in the gateway
options.pro: No change is needed in the services
options.con: Joins are written by hand in the gateway, and ownership of types is unclear

options.name: Federation with entity keys
options.pro: Services declare what they own and extend, and the planner does the joins
options.con: Needs composition, a router and discipline on keys

alternatives.pick: Federation, once more than a few teams own the schema.

alternatives.title: Where to avoid N+1

options.name: A call per parent object
options.con: Calls grow with the size of the answer

options.name: Batched entity lookups by key
options.pro: Calls depend only on the depth of the query
options.con: Each service must support a lookup by list of keys

options.name: Join in the database layer
options.con: Only works inside a service that owns all the data

alternatives.pick: Batched entity lookups between services and data loaders inside each service.

alternatives.title: How to limit abusive queries

options.name: Depth limit only
options.con: Wide, shallow queries still do huge work

options.name: Cost estimate with a budget
options.pro: Reflects the real work and works for any shape

options.name: Persisted queries only
options.pro: Only known and tested queries run
options.con: Fits first-party apps, not open public APIs

alternatives.pick: Persisted queries for first-party apps, and a cost budget for everything else, with a depth limit as a cheap extra.

alternatives.title: Who runs the gateway

options.name: A router in front of everything
options.pro: One place for plans, limits and tracing
options.con: A critical component to run and scale

options.name: Each client talks to the services
options.con: Clients must know the service layout and make the joins

alternatives.pick: A router that scales horizontally, with plans and schemas cached in memory.

roles.description: The batching window that collects the keys of each level into one call.

quiz.question: A client asks for 50 users, each with their 20 orders, each with a product. The router calls the orders service once per user and the products service once per order, so one request makes 1 + 50 + 1,000 calls, and it takes seconds. What is the correct fix?
options: Raise the connection pool size of the router and run all 1,050 calls in parallel, so that the sequential waits disappear
Cache each product response for 5 minutes by product id, so that repeated products need no new call to the service
Make the users service join orders and products inside its own database, so that only a single call is needed overall
Send all the keys of a level to the owning service in one entity lookup, so the calls depend on query depth and number 3 here
quiz.explanation: Batching by key turns calls proportional to the size of the answer into calls proportional to its depth. Parallel calls still load the services with 1,050 requests. A cache helps only repeated keys, and a join in one database works only when that service owns all the data, which it does not here.

quiz.question: A public API has a depth limit of 4. A client sends users(first: 100) { orders(first: 100) { items(first: 100) { product { name } } } }, which is depth 4 and passes. It would touch about a million items and starts to overload the services. What guard stops this class of query?
options: Lower the depth limit from 4 to 3, which is the level at which the large lists start to multiply into huge counts
Estimate cost by multiplying list sizes, cap each first argument, reject over-budget queries before any call
Add a rate limit of 10 requests per second per client, so that no single client can send a large number of such queries
Set a 2-second timeout on every subgraph call, so that slow and expensive queries are cancelled by the router quickly
quiz.explanation: Depth alone cannot see wide lists, and depth 3 here still means 100 x 100 x 100 items. A per-client request rate does not limit the size of one query. A timeout works only after the services have started the work, so rejecting on estimated cost has to come first.

quiz.question: The orders team wants to remove the field Order.legacyTotal. The schema check composes fine. Usage records from the last 30 days show 3% of requests still select it, all from an old mobile app version that many users have not updated. What should happen?
options: Remove it now, because composition passed, and ask the mobile team to force every user of the old app version to update soon
Remove it after a canary on one router shows no rise in errors, since routers can keep serving the old supergraph
Mark it deprecated, block removal in the schema check while usage is above zero, and remove it only when usage reaches zero
Keep serving the old supergraph on every router for a week after the removal, and retire it once the week has passed
quiz.explanation: Composition shows only that the supergraph is valid, not that real clients still use the field, so the check compares against actual operations. A canary of routers would not see the failing app versions either, and keeping the old supergraph only delays the same breakage.
